_comment: One rule, three implementations. 'What role is this user, really' is decided
in backend/utils/roles.py (get_effective_role / get_effective_roles), in
web/src/utils/userRoles.js for the web app, and in
mobile/src/utils/effectiveRole.ts for mobile. Both client copies say in
their own docstrings that they mirror the others.
They did not. On 2026-09-07 the mobile effectiveRoleOf read ONLY the legacy
org_role field and ignored org_roles entirely, where the server treats
org_roles as taking precedence -- so an org user whose roles live only in the
array would have resolved to the literal string 'org_managed' on a phone and
to their real role everywhere else. Latent rather than live: checked prod on
the day, and all 744 org-managed users carry org_role, with org_roles[0]
equal to it in all 14 multi-role cases. The rule still has to agree.
Expected values are GENERATED by running backend/utils/roles.py over these
inputs. The server is canonical: it is the one that decides what an endpoint
actually allows, and a client that disagrees offers a control whose save is
refused (see QF-01's useCanEditXp finding, same shape).
Each side has a test that reads this file. Adding a case here makes all three
prove they still agree.
server and a client: for {role:'org_managed', org_role:'advisor',
org_roles:['teacher']} the singular get_effective_role falls through to
org_role and says 'advisor', while get_effective_roles filters the array to
nothing and returns []. An empty roles list passes no role check at all, so
that account would resolve to a real role and still be refused everywhere.
It is unreachable through the database -- users.org_roles has a CHECK
constraint (valid_org_roles -> validate_org_roles()) that rejects an unknown
value -- so it is REPRODUCED here rather than corrected. Correcting it means
widening what the server allows, which is a decision for whoever owns the
authorization model.
One case here used to document a disagreement INSIDE the server: for
{role:'org_managed', org_role:'advisor', org_roles:['teacher']} the singular
get_effective_role fell through to org_role and said 'advisor', while
get_effective_roles filtered the array to nothing and returned []. An empty
roles list passes no role check at all, so that account resolved to a real
role and was refused everywhere. FIXED 2026-09-07: the plural now falls
through the same way, so both answer 'advisor'. It was unreachable through
the valid_org_roles CHECK constraint, which is why it had gone unnoticed --
the fix removes a lockout that depended on that constraint staying correct.

cases.why: a platform student carries their role directly
superadmin short-circuits everything else on the dict
an org user's real role is in org_role, not the org_managed placeholder
a campus coordinator -- org-only, never in users.role
org_roles alone resolves, with no legacy org_role present
org_roles TAKES PRECEDENCE over org_role when they disagree
a multi-role org user's primary role is the first of org_roles
...and every role in the array counts for a hasRole check
an org_roles value that is not a real org role is ignored
an org_role that is not a real org role falls back to student
an org user with neither field falls back to student
an empty org_roles array falls through to org_role
a user dict with no role at all is a student
